tests.name: NEW: GPU-residency guard blocks a double-start over an untracked resident process
tests.setup: a setsid'd fake 'python -u -m research.runners.faketest_orphan' process is spawned and NOT recorded anywhere in gpu.queue/gpu.running -- simulating a job orphaned by a dead dispatcher incarnation or a truly-standalone launch. A fake nvidia-smi script reports it as GPU-resident (compute-apps) while also reporting abundant free VRAM (99999 MiB), isolating the residency check from the pre-existing VRAM-threshold check.
checks: C1: with the residency guard ACTIVE, a second queued job does NOT run while the untracked process is 'resident'
C1b: the queued job is never popped from gpu.queue (peeks-don't-pops holds under the guard)

C2 (failing direction): with GPU_QUEUE_NO_RESIDENCY_GUARD=1 (test-only bypass), the SAME untracked process does NOT block the second job -- it double-starts -- proving C1 is testing the real mechanism, not a tautology

tests.name: NEW: pause --now reaches the genuinely-resident process despite a stale gpu.running record
tests.setup: a second setsid'd fake standalone process is spawned. gpu.running is deliberately written with an unrelated, already-dead pid (spawned and immediately reaped) as the 'recorded' job -- simulating totally lost tracking, the exact symptom reported ('gpu.running showed one pid while the actual GPU compute proc was a different pid').
checks: pause --now is invoked against this state; the genuinely GPU-resident process must be killed even though gpu.running's own record points nowhere useful
tests.result: PASS -- pause --now's target set is the union of (gpu.running's descendant tree) UNION (nvidia-smi's compute-apps residency scan), so the stale record no longer hides the real process
tests.sample_output: PAUSED + killed current job/process(es) (VRAM freed) [pids: 3139116 3139117]; re-queued it at the front for resume if it was a tracked job.

bugs_found_and_fixed_during_this_verific.bug: fd-8 (the singleton DLOCK) is inherited by every child the daemon forks (a fork inherits open fds by default). The dispatched job itself (setsid bash -c "$job") is the serious case: if the daemon dies mid-job, the orphaned job keeps the DLOCK open for its entire remaining runtime (hours, for multi-day campaigns), so a freshly-restarted daemon could never even win the singleton lock to reach the new residency guard -- silently defeating the fix in exactly the scenario it targets.
bugs_found_and_fixed_during_this_verific.found_via: --selftest TEST C initially failed to reproduce its own failing direction (C2); tracing with fuser/lsof showed the DLOCK held open by a `sleep` process, not the killed daemon.
bugs_found_and_fixed_during_this_verific.fix: 8>&- appended to every subprocess the daemon forks (sleep calls, the queue-pop subshell, and critically the dispatched job itself).

bugs_found_and_fixed_during_this_verific.bug: pause --now's kill loop ran under `set -e` (unlike daemon(), which explicitly disables it) and used bare `kill ... "$t" 2>/dev/null` statements. `2>/dev/null` only hides kill's error message, not its nonzero exit status when the target is already dead -- so the FIRST already-dead target in the list aborted the whole sweep, silently skipping every later target.
bugs_found_and_fixed_during_this_verific.found_via: --selftest TEST D's deliberately-stale gpu.running record (an intentionally already-dead pid) tripped this exact path; `bash -x` tracing showed execution stop dead after the failing kill with no further output.
bugs_found_and_fixed_during_this_verific.fix: every kill in the pause --now sweep is `|| true`-guarded.

bugs_found_and_fixed_during_this_verific.bug: the new pause --now target sweep did a process-GROUP-wide kill (`kill -TERM -pgid`) for every discovered pid unconditionally. A pid surfaced by the new GPU-residency scan has unknown provenance -- it need not be setsid-isolated -- so a group-wide kill on it could signal an entire unrelated process group (a user's shell/session).
bugs_found_and_fixed_during_this_verific.found_via: a selftest test process that was NOT setsid'd shared its process group with the selftest script itself; pause --now's group-kill hit that shared group and truncated the whole test run's output.
bugs_found_and_fixed_during_this_verific.fix: group-kill (`-pgid`) now fires only when the target IS confirmed to be its own process-group leader (pgid == its own pid); otherwise only the specific pid is signalled.
